Net burn stays the same every month.
Cash on hand is the money in the bank today, not money owed to the company.
Net burn is cash out less cash in over a month, so a month with no net burn has no runway to count.
The first month uses the net burn you entered.
Each later month uses the month before it multiplied by 1 plus the growth percent divided by 100.
Add up the months until the next one would use more than the cash left.
Runway is the whole months funded plus the cash left divided by that next month’s burn, rounded down to one decimal place.
Burn grows by the same percent every month.
A burn that falls is not modeled.

The calculator works in your browser.

The page makes no request after it loads, and you can confirm that in your browser's network panel.
What the results are not
The results are arithmetic on the numbers you typed.
They are not advice, a forecast, or a statement about whether anyone will invest, and WE makes no promise of funding.
The calculator cannot tell whether an entry is right.
It does not say how much runway is enough, because that depends on your plan and no source supports a number.
Level burn and growing burn
Runway at level burn tells you what happens if nothing changes, and something will.
It is the same division the metrics calculator uses for runway.
The second result lets you try a burn that grows by a percent each month, and the working shows each step so you can check it by hand.
Round down
Runway is rounded down to one decimal place, because a figure rounded up flatters the position.

Your numbers stay on this page
The explainer works in your browser.
It sends nothing, it saves nothing, and it does not put your numbers in the address bar, so closing the tab removes them.
The page makes no request after it loads, and you can confirm that in your browser's network panel.
What the results are not
The results are arithmetic on the numbers you typed.
They are not advice, a forecast, or a statement about whether anyone will invest, and WE makes no promise of funding.
The explainer cannot tell whether an entry matches your signed documents.
It counts shares only, so it cannot tell you what to issue, to whom or on what terms.
How issuing shares changes ownership
Your ownership is the number of shares you hold divided by all the shares issued.
When the company issues new shares to someone else, the number you hold stays the same, but it becomes a smaller part of a larger total, so your ownership falls.
That fall is often called dilution.
The explainer shows each division and the change, so you can check them by hand.
What it counts and leaves out
The explainer counts issued shares only.
Options, promised options and any other right to shares are left out, because they are not yet shares.
A fully diluted count adds them in.
The article on cap table basics explains what that count contains.
